title: Ashesi Orientation + Campus Tour + iGEM
purpose: Introduce the course as place-based and collaborative learning.
key_learning: Learning did not only happen in classrooms; it happened through partnership, movement, observation, and dialogue.
course_concept: Place-based learning; collaborative knowledge production; academic exchange.
reflection: Starting at Ashesi made the course feel less like studying Ghana from outside and more like learning with people, institutions, and peers already embedded in the context. The campus itself became a site of learning before we even left the gates.
what_happened: We arrived at Ashesi University in Berekuso, met our iGEM student collaborators, toured the campus, and were briefed on the course structure and collaborative learning approach.
systems_insight: The course itself was designed as a system — learning through place, relationship, and movement, not just lectures or textbooks.
reading_tie: Course introduction readings; place-based education; collaborative learning frameworks

title: Introduction to Water Security + Faircap Water Quality Activity
purpose: Introduce water quality, contamination, and point-of-use treatment.
key_learning: Safe water depends on both technical treatment and everyday access and use. Testing makes invisible risk visible.
course_concept: Improved source does not always mean safe, reliable, or sufficient water.
reflection: I started to see how something that looks clean can still carry risk, and how water safety depends on barriers from source to consumption. The Faircap filter turned an abstract lecture into something I could hold.
what_happened: We attended a lecture on water security and then used Faircap filters and water quality test strips to test water samples from different sources on campus.
systems_insight: Improved source water is not the same as safe water. Treatment must happen across the full path from source to mouth — and testing makes invisible risk visible.
reading_tie: WHO drinking water quality guidelines; point-of-use treatment evidence; Faircap filter design

title: Lavender Hill / Fecal Sludge Management
purpose: Show sanitation as a full chain, not just a toilet.
key_learning: Sanitation can break at containment, emptying, transport, treatment, reuse, regulation, or financing.
course_concept: Fecal sludge management; resource recovery; sanitation chain.
reflection: This stop shifted my view of sanitation from a household issue to an urban systems issue. The smell, the scale, the people working there — it made the sanitation chain real in a way no diagram could.
what_happened: We visited Lavender Hill, a fecal sludge management and processing facility in Accra, and spoke with operators about the full sanitation chain from household to treatment site.
systems_insight: Sanitation is a full chain, not just a toilet. It can break at containment, emptying, transport, treatment, reuse, regulation, or financing — and each failure has consequences.
reading_tie: Fecal sludge management literature; sanitation chain; resource recovery from waste

title: Arts Market + Kwame Nkrumah Memorial
purpose: Situate water, environment, and health systems within Ghana's political and historical context.
key_learning: Technical systems are shaped by history, identity, national development, markets, and politics.
reflection: This helped me remember that infrastructure is never separate from history or power. The memorial and the market exist in the same city as broken pipes and open drains — they are part of the same story.
what_happened: We visited the Accra Arts Market and the Kwame Nkrumah Mausoleum and Memorial Park, learning about Ghana's history of independence and political identity.
systems_insight: Technical systems do not exist apart from history. Infrastructure is shaped by colonial legacy, national identity, markets, and politics — not only engineering.
reading_tie: Ghana's political history; Kwame Nkrumah and Pan-Africanism; development in postcolonial context

title: Water for Health Lecture + Local Health Clinic
purpose: Connect WASH to healthcare access and health geography.
key_learning: Water insecurity affects health through disease, stress, infrastructure gaps, transport barriers, and uneven access to care.
course_concept: Health as physical, mental, and social well-being; waterborne, water-washed, water-based, and water-related disease.
reflection: Seeing the clinic made the health impacts of WASH feel more concrete. It was not just about disease pathways, but also about roads, staffing, insurance, transport, and the limits of reactive healthcare.
what_happened: We attended a lecture on water, sanitation, and health linkages, then visited a local health clinic to see primary care access in context.
systems_insight: Water insecurity affects health through disease, stress, and infrastructure gaps — but health access also depends on roads, staffing, insurance, and transport, not just water quality.
reading_tie: Water-related disease typology (F-diagram); health geography; primary healthcare access in LMICs

title: Berekuso Spiritual Stream
purpose: Show that water is also cultural, spiritual, and governed through local authority.
key_learning: Water systems are shaped by land, tradition, authority, belief, ownership, and environmental change.
course_concept: Hydrosocial cycle; local environmental governance; cultural meanings of water.
reflection: The stream challenged me to think about water not only as a resource to manage, but as something tied to identity, place, and authority. The chief's role in protecting it was as real as any pipe or pump.
what_happened: We visited a spiritually significant stream near Berekuso, protected through the authority of local chiefs and traditional governance structures.
systems_insight: Water is not only a resource to be managed. It is also sacred, identity-forming, and governed through cultural authority as much as through formal policy or technical systems.
reading_tie: Hydrosocial cycle theory; cultural and spiritual meanings of water; local environmental governance

title: WASHKing / Decentralized Sanitation
purpose: Connect technical sanitation design with local enterprise and decentralized service models.
key_learning: Decentralized sanitation depends on design, maintenance, affordability, user acceptance, and business models.
reflection: This stop made me think about whether a technology is actually appropriate if it cannot be maintained, financed, or adopted by the people meant to use it. A working toilet that nobody uses is not a success.
what_happened: We visited a WASHKing enterprise and saw their prefabricated latrine slabs and decentralized sanitation business model in action.
systems_insight: Appropriate technology must be maintainable, affordable, and accepted by the people who will use it. A toilet no one can fix or afford is not a solution.
reading_tie: Appropriate technology; hardware and software in WASH; community-led sanitation; sanitation enterprise models

title: Aquaya Guest Lecture + Ashesi Research Symposium
purpose: Show the role of data, finance, benchmarking, and accountability in WASH systems.
key_learning: Water systems can fail not because the technology is absent, but because data, money, staffing, and accountability systems are weak.
course_concept: Rural water finance; mWater; KPIs; performance benchmarking; data gaps.
reflection: This helped me see that reliability is not only technical. It is also financial and institutional. A well that nobody has money to fix is a broken well, even if the pump still works.
what_happened: We attended an Aquaya guest lecture on rural water finance and data systems, and visited the Ashesi Research Symposium on WASH innovation and monitoring.
systems_insight: Water systems can fail not because technology is absent, but because data, money, staffing, and accountability systems are weak. Reliability is institutional, not only technical.
reading_tie: Rural water finance; mWater data platform; KPIs for water services; performance benchmarking in WASH

title: GWCL Weija Treatment Plant + Ghana Water Institute
purpose: Demonstrate centralized water treatment and technical capacity.
key_learning: Safe drinking water depends on treatment steps, monitoring, trained staff, maintenance, and distribution.
course_concept: Multiple-barrier treatment; coagulation; flocculation; filtration; disinfection; residual chlorine.
reflection: This stop made the technical side of WASH visible, but it also showed that infrastructure is only one part of the system. A treatment plant does not help a household that cannot afford the connection.
what_happened: We toured the GWCL Weija Water Treatment Plant and Ghana Water Institute, seeing the full multi-barrier treatment process for Accra's water supply.
systems_insight: Safe drinking water at scale requires treatment steps, trained operators, monitoring, and reliable distribution — and each step can fail independently.
reading_tie: Multiple-barrier treatment; coagulation; flocculation; sedimentation; filtration; chlorination; residual chlorine monitoring

title: Accra School of Hygiene + Community Visit
purpose: Connect WASH to hygiene promotion, public health education, and community-level practice.
key_learning: Behaviour change and community engagement are part of WASH infrastructure, not an optional add-on.
course_concept: Software side of WASH; hygiene promotion; F-diagram barriers.
reflection: This stop helped me see why a technically correct intervention can still fail if people are not included, trained, or supported. The handwashing station in the school was the most used piece of infrastructure we saw.
what_happened: We visited the Accra School of Hygiene and a nearby community site to observe hygiene promotion, WASH education, and community-level practice in action.
systems_insight: Behaviour change is part of the WASH system, not optional. A technically correct intervention can fail if people are not included, trained, and supported.
reading_tie: F-diagram barriers to fecal-oral disease transmission; hygiene promotion theory and practice; WASH software

title: Cape Coast / Elmina Castle
purpose: Reflect on history, power, colonialism, and inequality as structural forces.
key_learning: Field learning requires attention to historical systems that continue to shape present-day inequities.
course_concept: Power, place, colonial history, development context.
reflection: This stop widened the frame of the course. It reminded me that present-day systems are built on historical foundations, including violence, extraction, and unequal power. Water access today is not separate from that history.
what_happened: We visited the Cape Coast area and toured Elmina Castle, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and major site of the Atlantic slave trade.
systems_insight: Present-day WASH inequities are built on historical foundations — including systems of extraction, colonialism, and unequal power. Ignoring this history limits what we can understand about the present.
reading_tie: Colonial history of West Africa; Atlantic slave trade; development in postcolonial context; power and place

title: CEWEFIA / Gender and WASH
purpose: Connect WASH to gendered labour, safety, dignity, and community knowledge.
key_learning: WASH burdens are not distributed equally. Women and girls often carry responsibility for water, hygiene, care work, and household adaptation when systems fail.
course_concept: Gendered WASH; care work; social vulnerability; women's participation in decision-making.
reflection: This was one of the strongest reminders that infrastructure can look successful on paper while still ignoring who carries the daily burden of making it work. The jug full of water is invisible in most datasets.
what_happened: We met with CEWEFIA, a women's organization working on gender and WASH integration, and discussed water collection burdens, safety, and care work.
systems_insight: WASH burdens are not equally shared. Women and girls carry disproportionate responsibility for water, hygiene, and care work — especially when formal systems fail.
reading_tie: Gendered WASH; care work and time poverty; women's participation in WASH governance; social vulnerability

title: Sacred Forest + UCC Community Visit
purpose: Bring Indigenous and local environmental perspectives into the WASH and environment discussion.
key_learning: Environmental knowledge is not only technical or scientific. It can also be cultural, spiritual, historical, and community-held.
course_concept: Indigenous perspectives; environmental governance; multiple ways of knowing.
reflection: This stop helped me question what counts as expertise and who gets treated as a legitimate environmental knowledge-holder. The forest was governed long before any government agency wrote a policy about it.
what_happened: We visited a sacred forest near Cape Coast that is protected through community governance, and attended a UCC community visit on local environmental knowledge.
systems_insight: Communities have governed forests and water for generations before formal policy. Indigenous and local environmental knowledge is not informal or lesser — it is a different kind of expertise.
reading_tie: Indigenous environmental knowledge; multiple ways of knowing; community-based conservation; environmental governance

title: Kakum National Park
purpose: Connect forests, biodiversity, tourism, water, and environmental protection.
key_learning: Human health, ecosystems, land use, water, and livelihoods are interconnected.
course_concept: Ecosystem health; climate resilience; conservation; environmental systems.
reflection: Kakum helped me think beyond WASH facilities and toward the landscapes that shape water, climate, and life. The trees hold the rain. The rain fills the streams. The streams feed the wells.
what_happened: We walked the canopy walkway at Kakum National Park and discussed how forest cover, rainfall, and ecosystem health connect to water availability and livelihoods.
systems_insight: Human health, ecosystems, land use, water, and livelihoods are not separate. Forests hold rain, rain fills streams, streams feed wells — and deforestation breaks this.
reading_tie: Ecosystem services; forest and water linkages; climate resilience; conservation biology

title: Photo-Elicitation Exercise + Cape Coast Debrief
purpose: Show how method affects what knowledge becomes visible.
key_learning: Photos and stories can reveal lived experiences that surveys or technical reports may miss.
course_concept: Photovoice; photo-elicitation; social constructivism; multiple perspectives.
reflection: This stop helped me see knowledge mobilization as more than explaining facts. It is also about creating formats where different perspectives can be seen and heard. This game is, in part, a response to that lesson.
what_happened: We completed a photo-elicitation exercise where course participants selected images from the journey and shared what they revealed about WASH, then held a group debrief in Cape Coast.
systems_insight: What counts as data? Method shapes what knowledge becomes visible. Photos and stories can reveal lived experiences that technical surveys and reports often miss.
reading_tie: Photovoice methodology; photo-elicitation; social constructivism; participatory research methods

title: Tetteh Quashie Cocoa Farm
purpose: Connect water, agriculture, climate, history, and economic survival.
key_learning: Water security is connected to food systems, livelihoods, land, climate variability, and colonial and global commodity histories.
course_concept: Water-food-livelihood linkages; climate impacts; agricultural systems.
reflection: The cocoa farm made the course feel more connected. WASH is not separate from food, income, farming, land, or climate. It is part of how people live. The cocoa pod holds water, history, and survival in one shape.
what_happened: We visited the Tetteh Quashie Cocoa Farm and learned about Ghana's cocoa history, smallholder farming, climate vulnerability, and how water connects to food and income.
systems_insight: Water security cannot be separated from food, income, climate, and land. How people survive shapes how they use and value water — and climate change threatens all of it at once.
reading_tie: Water-food-livelihood nexus; cocoa farming in Ghana; climate impacts on smallholder agriculture; global commodity chains
